extracted.intended_audience: scientists, researchers, and general readers interested in academic publishing and research integrity
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative criteria and behavioral guidance about publishing in high‑impact ('luxury') journals, covering what journals claim they evaluate (significance, peer review), and critiques of prestige-based incentives that may harm research quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection based on scientific significance
rubrics_metrics.description: "We select research for publication in Nature on the basis of scientific significance."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals (as stated by editors) claim they choose papers primarily for scientific significance; this is presented as the principled basis for accepting work. Use significance as an explicit selection criterion when evaluating submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough and professional peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: "Our editorial staff is dedicated to ensuring a thorough and professional peer review upon which they determine which papers to select for inclusion in our journal."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors justify selection by the rigor and professionalism of the peer‑review process. A criterion for publication is evidence of having passed careful review; thorough peer review is offered as a quality control mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance rate reflects scope and mission
rubrics_metrics.description: "There is nothing artificial about the acceptance rate. It reflects the scope and mission of our journal."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Low acceptance is framed as a deliberate consequence of a journal's defined scope/mission rather than an arbitrary gatekeeping mechanism. When judging selectivity, consider mission alignment as a stated rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic constraints on publishing volume
rubrics_metrics.description: "We have a large circulation and printing additional papers has a real economic cost."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical economic limits (print/circulation costs) are offered as a reason for limited publication slots. Resource constraints can legitimately influence how many papers a journal publishes, which affects acceptance decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of the science matters, not the journal's brand
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is the quality of the science, not the journal's brand, that matters."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocated as a normative criterion for evaluating research: assess work by its intrinsic scientific merit rather than the prestige of the outlet. This is a recommended principle for researchers, reviewers, and institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journals reward 'trendy' or 'flashy' work over important work (critical claim)
rubrics_metrics.description: Schekman's accusation that journals "encourag[e] scientists to pursue 'trendy' fields of science and reward the 'flashiest work, not the best'".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an evaluative critique: when judging journals or publication incentives, watch for preference toward novelty/flash over robustness/importance. Anti‑pattern: valuing trendiness can misdirect research priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limiting number of articles to create brand demand (branding tyranny)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparison of luxury journals to designers who "create limited‑edition handbags or suits by restricting the number of articles they print in a bid to create demand for the 'brand'."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes a practice where scarcity is used to cultivate prestige. As a criterion, examine whether editorial limits are serving scientific selection or manufacturing exclusivity for brand value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lure of prestige can encourage cutting corners and increase retractions
rubrics_metrics.description: "In extreme cases the lure of the luxury journal can encourage the cutting of corners, and contribute to the escalating number of papers that are retracted as flawed or fraudulent."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifies a causal link between prestige incentives and compromised research practices. Use incidence of retractions, signs of rushed/unsound methods, or evidence of misconduct as negative indicators tied to prestige pressures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioral remedy: scientists avoiding luxury journals
rubrics_metrics.description: "I have now committed my lab to avoiding luxury journals, and I encourage others to do likewise."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed action as a normative criterion: individual labs and researchers can change incentives by refusing to play prestige games. For producing work, choice of venue becomes an ethical/strategic decision aimed at altering community norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prestige and historical longevity as justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Editor Philip Campbell noting that being in print for 140 years "proved its support of the scientific community."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals may invoke historical longevity and prestige to justify practices. When evaluating journals or using venue as a proxy for quality, be aware of appeals to tradition which may not equate to current scientific rigor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systemic incentives analogy (bonus culture) — incentive structure matters
rubrics_metrics.description: "Like many successful researchers, I have published in the big brands... Just as Wall Street needs to break the hold of the bonus culture... so science must break the tyranny of the luxury journals."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames publication incentives as part of a broader systemic incentives problem. Criterion for reform: assess and modify incentive structures (promotion, hiring, funding) that reward publishing in prestige venues rather than substantive scientific contributions.
